prompt: Quitanda attaches the bucket `quitanda-raw-prod` to a raw zone of a Dataplex lake. What happens to the objects in it?
hint: Dataplex describes data; does it hold any?

choices.text: They are copied into storage the lake manages
choices.why: Dataplex stores no data; the lake is a description over buckets and datasets that stay where they are.

choices.text: Nothing: it stays the same bucket, in place
choices.why: Right. An asset is a reference to a real bucket or dataset, and not a byte of it moves.

choices.text: They are converted to Parquet, the curated format
choices.why: Formats change only when a job rewrites the data; a raw zone holds data as it arrived.

choices.text: They become readable only through Dataplex
choices.why: IAM on the bucket still decides who reads it, zone or no zone.

prompt: An analyst has `storage.objects.get` on `quitanda-curated-prod` through IAM, and the bucket is an asset of a curated zone the analyst was never granted. Can the analyst read the files with `gcloud storage cat`?
hint: Does a zone replace IAM, or manage it?

choices.text: No, because the zone's grants take precedence over the bucket's
choices.why: A zone has no permission system of its own that overrides IAM; it manages IAM bindings on its assets.

choices.text: No, because files in a zone are reachable only through BigQuery
choices.why: The files are ordinary objects, and Cloud Storage serves them to whoever IAM allows.

choices.text: Yes, because IAM on the bucket still decides who reads it
choices.why: Right. Dataplex manages bindings for you; it does not interpose itself between a reader and the bucket.

choices.text: Yes, but only the files discovery has not catalogued yet
choices.why: Discovery decides what appears as tables, not who may read objects.

prompt: Match each piece of Quitanda's estate to the Dataplex concept it is.
hint: From the outermost box to the real things inside it.

pairs.left: where data lands as it arrived
where cleaned data held to a schema lives

prompt: The documentation you find says "Data Catalog", a colleague says "Dataplex Universal Catalog", and the pricing page says "Knowledge Catalog". What should you conclude?
hint: Read the table of names in the section.

choices.text: They are three competing products to choose between
choices.why: They are one line of descent; the older name is deprecated in favour of the newer.

choices.text: Mostly one product, renamed as it grew, so check the date of what you read
choices.why: Right. The names changed on Google's schedule, and the page read on 2026-10-30 says the SKUs still say Dataplex.

choices.text: Only Knowledge Catalog exists, so the other pages are fabricated
choices.why: The older names were real products; renaming does not erase their documentation.

choices.text: Data Catalog is the newest, since it is the simplest name
choices.why: It is the oldest of the three, and the one being retired.

prompt: Quitanda creates a new BigQuery table. What has to happen before it can be found in the catalog's search?
hint: Where do entries for Google Cloud's own services come from?

choices.text: Somebody registers it as a custom entry
choices.why: Custom entries are for things outside Google Cloud; BigQuery's are ingested.

choices.text: Nothing; its entry appears there on its own
choices.why: Right. Technical metadata from BigQuery is ingested automatically, into the system entry group `@bigquery`.

choices.text: A discovery scan has to run over its dataset
choices.why: Discovery reads files in buckets; a BigQuery table already has its metadata in BigQuery.

choices.text: An aspect type has to be defined for it
choices.why: Aspects add meaning to an entry; the entry exists without any.

prompt: Quitanda writes an `ownership` aspect on a table and leaves out `owner_team`, which the aspect type marks as required. What happens?
hint: What is the difference between a structured aspect and a wiki page?

choices.text: The aspect is written, and a later scan flags it
choices.why: Nothing waits for a scan; the type is checked when the aspect is written.

choices.text: The aspect is written with an empty owner
choices.why: A required field has no empty default; leaving it out is the error.

choices.text: It is refused, and nothing reaches the catalog
choices.why: Right. The aspect type is a schema, and a value that breaks it is refused, which is what keeps the metadata structured.

choices.text: The table is hidden from search until it is fixed
choices.why: Aspects describe an entry; a bad one is refused, it does not hide the table.

prompt: Somebody edits the catalog entry of `curated.orders` so that its description says a column was dropped, and nothing else changes. What do BigQuery queries on the table do?
hint: Where does BigQuery read a table's schema from?

choices.text: They fail on the column the description says is gone
choices.why: BigQuery does not read the catalog to plan a query; the description changes nothing it does.

choices.text: They run exactly as before
choices.why: Right. The catalog is an index over BigQuery's own metadata, so a wrong description misleads people and breaks no query.

choices.text: They return the column empty until the entry is corrected
choices.why: The column's data is in BigQuery's storage, untouched by any catalog text.

choices.text: They are refused until the schema and the entry agree
choices.why: No check compares the two; that is why the catalog's accuracy is a matter of discipline.

prompt: In the older Data Catalog, a tag followed a tag template; in Dataplex's catalog the same structured metadata is an ___, and its template is an ___ type.
hint: One word, the same in both blanks.

prompt: What does a data profile scan tell you that a data quality scan does not, and the other way round?
hint: One describes, one judges.

choices.text: The profile describes each column; the quality scan passes or fails rules
choices.why: Right. A profile reports nulls, distinct values and ranges; quality rules turn expectations into pass or fail.

choices.text: The profile checks the schema; the quality scan checks the rows
choices.why: Both look at the rows; the difference is between describing them and judging them.

choices.text: The profile runs once; the quality scan only runs on a schedule
choices.why: Either can run on demand or on a schedule.

choices.text: The profile is free, and only the quality scan is billed
choices.why: Both are billed as premium processing, by the DCU-hour.

prompt: A rule's condition is true for 1,940 of 2,000 rows. What is the highest threshold, in percent, at which the rule still passes?
hint: The rule passes when the share of passing rows reaches the threshold.

prompt: In `scan.py`, why did the range rule on `total_cents` count the order with no total as a failure?
hint: What is `NULL BETWEEN 1 AND 500000`?

choices.text: Because DuckDB reads an empty field as zero
choices.why: The empty field was read as null; the profile counted it as 5.0% null.

choices.text: Because the range rule runs the non-null rule first
choices.why: Each rule is evaluated on its own; there is no order between them.

choices.text: A condition on a null is not true, and only true passes
choices.why: Right. The comparison is neither true nor false, so the row does not count as passing, as Dataplex treats nulls unless a rule says to ignore them.

choices.text: Because -500 and the null are the same row
choices.why: They are two different orders, `o-10013` and `o-10004`.

prompt: The phone rule passes every night at a threshold of 95%, and over three months the share of good numbers slides from 99% to 95.2%. What does the nightly pass or fail tell the team?
hint: What does a threshold hide?

choices.text: That something is wrong, since a rule warns before it fails
choices.why: A rule has two answers, pass and fail; it said pass every night.

choices.text: Nothing; the decline shows only if the results are kept and compared
choices.why: Right. The verdict hid a slide of almost four points, which is why scan results are kept and read as a series.

choices.text: That the threshold is too strict and should be lowered
choices.why: Lowering it would hide the decline for longer.

choices.text: That the scan is broken, since the numbers keep changing
choices.why: Changing numbers are the data changing; the scan reported them correctly.

prompt: The finance export for 1 October has wrong numbers. Which lineage question finds where they came from?
hint: Follow the arrows backwards or forwards?

choices.text: Downstream from the export
choices.why: Downstream from the export is what was made from it, and nothing was.

choices.text: Upstream from the export
choices.why: Right. `edges.py upstream` walked back through `daily_revenue` and `load_orders` to the raw CSV and the customers table.

choices.text: Upstream from the raw orders file
choices.why: The raw file has nothing upstream in this graph; it is where the walk ends.

choices.text: A search of the catalog for "finance"
choices.why: Search finds the export's entry; it does not say what it was made from.

prompt: A job reads three tables and writes two. Its completed run event becomes how many edges in `edges.py`'s graph?
hint: Every pair of one input and one output is an edge.

prompt: One job reports its output as `planner-dev.curated.orders` and the next reports its input as `planner-dev:curated.orders`, with a colon. What does the lineage graph show?
hint: How do two events agree that they touched the same table?

choices.text: One table, because the service normalises the separator
choices.why: Names are compared as written; nothing in the events says the two spellings mean one table.

choices.text: An error, because the second name is invalid
choices.why: Both are strings an event can carry; nothing refuses either.

choices.text: Two disconnected nodes, and a break in the graph
choices.why: Right. The name is the whole join, so the walk upstream from the second job stops at a table that seems to come from nowhere.

choices.text: Both nodes, joined by an edge the service infers
choices.why: No edge is inferred between two names; an edge comes only from a job's inputs and outputs.

prompt: By the Dataplex pricing page, which of these is billed?
hint: Who does the work of finding the links?

choices.text: Sending OpenLineage events with `ProcessOpenLineageRunEvent`
choices.why: The page calls this custom lineage and says it is free.

choices.text: Reading lineage back with the API's get and list methods
choices.why: The page says retrieving lineage is free.

choices.text: Automatic lineage parsing of BigQuery jobs
choices.why: Right. Google spends compute reading the jobs to find the links, and bills it as premium processing in DCU-hours.

choices.text: Reporting processes and runs from a custom client
choices.why: The page says reporting process metadata is free.

prompt: `phone` carries a policy tag with access control on, and an analyst without Fine-Grained Reader runs `SELECT * FROM curated.orders`. What happens?
hint: Is the column hidden, or is the query refused?

choices.text: The query fails with an access error on `phone`
choices.why: Right. Naming the column, which `*` does, is refused; `SELECT * EXCEPT (phone)` runs.

choices.text: The query runs and `phone` comes back null
choices.why: That is masking, which needs a data policy and the Masked Reader role; without it the query is refused.

choices.text: The query runs without the `phone` column
choices.why: BigQuery does not drop a column silently; the analyst has to leave it out.

choices.text: The query runs, because `*` names no column by name
choices.why: `*` names every column, `phone` included.

prompt: Analysts are given the SHA-256 mask of `phone` so they can group orders by customer phone. Why is that not anonymisation?
hint: What can anybody do with a list of every phone number in the city?

choices.text: Because SHA-256 can be decrypted with the right key
choices.why: A hash has no key and cannot be decrypted; the weakness is elsewhere.

choices.text: Because the mask is removed when the query is exported
choices.why: The mask applies to what the query returns, exports included.

choices.text: Because masked values are visible to Fine-Grained Readers
choices.why: They see the real values by design; that is not what makes the hash weak.

choices.text: Because anyone can hash every possible number and match them
choices.why: Right. Phone numbers are few enough to hash them all, and a deterministic hash then maps straight back.

prompt: Quitanda has both an `ownership` aspect saying `contains_personal_data` on `curated.orders` and a policy tag on `phone`. What does each one do?
hint: One is metadata, one is enforcement.

choices.text: The aspect tells people; the tag makes BigQuery refuse it
choices.why: Right. The aspect is found in search; the tag is checked on every query.

choices.text: Both make BigQuery refuse the column, so one is redundant
choices.why: An aspect is metadata; no engine enforces it.

choices.text: The aspect masks the column, and the tag documents it
choices.why: Masking is a data policy on a policy tag; an aspect only describes.

choices.text: The tag hides the table from search, and the aspect grants access
choices.why: Neither does either; search follows IAM, and grants are IAM roles.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson actually run, rather than take from Google's documentation? Choose every one it ran.
hint: Two programs ran, and both were models.

choices.text: Four quality rules computed over twenty orders with DuckDB
choices.why: Yes, `scan.py`, as a model of what a Dataplex rule computes.

choices.text: An upstream walk over a graph built from OpenLineage events
choices.why: Yes, `edges.py`, as a model of what the lineage service answers.

choices.text: A lake with a raw and a curated zone
choices.why: The `gcloud dataplex` commands were shown and not run; there is no emulator.

choices.text: A query refused by a policy tag on `phone`
choices.why: Policy tags were taught from the documentation; no BigQuery ran here.

choices.text: An event sent to `processOpenLineageRunEvent`
choices.why: The request was shown and not run; the events stayed in files.

prompt: Last night's raw orders file was loaded twice. Put the steps of handling it in a sensible order.
hint: Find the damage before repairing it, and prevent the next one last.
items: Confirm the duplicates with a uniqueness rule on `order_id`
Walk the lineage downstream from the raw file
Rerun the jobs that made each affected table and export
Add the uniqueness rule to the nightly quality scan
